snippet.text: The vomeronasal organ in rodents is an important social and sexual signaling pathway. We have investigated whether the housing of intact immature females in close proximity to mature males would interfere with the sensitivity of the immature rodent uterotrophic bioassay as the result of vomeronasal signals transmitted by male urinary proteins. The hypothesis was that the proximity of males might induce early puberty, thereby increasing mean uterine weight and reducing the responsiveness of the assay. The hypothesis was tested in both rats and mice by housing mature males above immature females, separated only by a wire screen, for 3 days and determining possible changes in uterine weight. The results were negative. Neither the mean uterine weight nor the group mean standard deviation of the uterine weights were changed in the uterotrophic bioassay. Given that the timing of sexual maturation may vary with the strain of mouse used, we also evaluated the sensitivity of the immature mouse uterotrophic assay to diethylstilbestrol (DES) using four strains of mice. Similar sensitivity was observed for the CD-1, C57Bl6, and Alpk strains, but B6CBF(1) mice were marginally less sensitive to DES than were the other strains. These findings add to earlier data indicating the robustness of the rodent uterotrophic assay protocol.

documents.title: Lessons learned, challenges, and opportunities: the U.S. Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program.
documents.snippet:
Leah Zorrilla, Carolyn Favaro, Kelli Davis, Jeffrey P. Davis, Susan Borghoff Integrated Laboratory Systems, Inc., Research Triangle Park, NC 27709 The U.S. EPA Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program (EDSP) includes four in vivo mammalian assays to screen test substances for potential disruption of the estrogen, androgen, or thyroid hormone pathways. 

The Uterotrophic Assay screens for potential estrogenic activity and can be performed in immature intact females or ovariectomized adult rats. Animals are administered the test substance for three days, and at termination the wet and blotted uterine weights are obtained. A positive estrogenic response in the assay is a significant increase in the uterine weights. The performance criteria (vehicle control blotted uterine weights as a percent of body weight) were met in all studies conducted in either animal model. The Hershberger Bioassay screens for both potential androgenic and anti-androgenic activity in the adult male castrated rat. Animals are administered test substance for ten consecutive days and at termination five androgen-dependent tissues (glans penis, ventral prostate, seminal vesicle, Cowper's gland, and levator ani plus bulbocavernosus muscle) are excised and weighed. A positive response in the agonist assay or antagonist assay is a significant increase or decrease, respectively, in at least two tissue weights compared to controls. The performance criteria (no more than 2 of 10 tissues at or below coefficient of variation in control and high dose groups) were met in all assays. We demonstrate that the performance criteria in the Uterotrophic and Hershberger Assays are attainable and repeatable in our laboratory, and multiple vehicles may be used to administer the test substance without concern of meeting the performance criteria.

Title: Endocrine Disruptors and the Thyroid Gland—A Combined in Vitro and in Vivo Analysis of Potential New Biomarkers
Snippet: Assays currently being used to address thyroid-disrupting effects were developed from existing protocols for detecting general toxicologic effects of substances. These assays measure biochemical, clinical, hematologic, histologic, neurologic, behavioral, reproductive, and developmental end points. To address thyroid toxicity, the ability to determine several thyroid-relevant parameters was incorporated into these tests. Examples are the male and female pubertal assays as developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency [Endocrine Disruptor Screening and Testing Advisory Committee (EDSTAC) 1998] and the enhanced Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Test Guideline 407 (Gelbke et al. 2004). Currently, end points describing thyroid function, that is, serum T 4 , T 3 , and thyrotropin (TSH) as well as thyroid weight and histology, are being assessed according to these protocols. 

An amphibian assay (XEMA) based on the T 3 -dependent metamorphosis of tadpoles using the model X. laevis has been developed and is now being validated (Degitz et al. 2005;Opitz et al. 2006). This assay examines, for example, tail resorption, forelimb emergence, histologic alterations in the thyroid gland, and TSH expression. No sufficiently developed assay or standardized, validated protocol exists for the assessment of thyroid function in birds or fish nor is there any functional in vitro screening test for antithyroid action. Whether EDCs affect thyroid hormone economy and action in invertebrates, which do not have thyroid tissue organized as a gland composed of follicles (amphibians, birds, mammals) or at least single thyroid hormone-producing follicles (fish), has not been determined. An extensive overview of testing protocols used to determine thyroid toxicants is published by the OECD Environment Directorate and is available on the OECD website (BATTELLE 2006).

Title: Endocrine Disruptors and the Thyroid Gland—A Combined in Vitro and in Vivo Analysis of Potential New Biomarkers
Snippet: Background There is growing evidence that, in addition to the reproductive system, the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis is a target of endocrine-disrupting compounds (EDCs). However, this is not reflected adequately in current screening and assessment procedures for endocrine activity that to date determine only general parameters of thyroid function. Objective and Methods We used several in vitro and ex vivo assays in an attempt to identify suitable biomarkers for antithyroid action testing a selected panel of putative EDCs. Results In vitro we detected stimulation or inhibition of iodide uptake into FRTL-5 rat thyroid cells, inhibition of thyroid hormone binding to transthyretin, agonistic or antagonistic effects in a thyroid hormone receptor–dependent reporter assay, and inhibition of thyroid peroxidase using a novel assay system based on human recombinant thyroperoxidase that might be suitable for routine screening for potential EDCs. In rats, chronic application of several EDCs led to changes in thyroid morphology, alterations of thyrotropin and thyroid hormone serum levels as well as alterations in peripheral thyroid hormone–regulated end points such as malic enzyme and type I 5′-deiodinase activity. Conclusions As the effects of EDCs do not reflect classic mechanisms of hormone-dependent regulation and feedback, we believe multitarget and multimodal actions of EDCs affect the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis. These complex effects require a diverse approach for screening, evaluation, and risk assessment of potential antithyroid compounds. This approach involves novel in vitro or cell-based screening assays in order to assess thyroid hormone synthesis, transport, metabolism, and action as well as in vivo assays to measure thyroid hormone–regulated tissue-specific and developmental end points in animals.

Title: Clues from wildlife to create an assay for thyroid system disruption.
Snippet: In 1996 the U.S. Congress charged the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to develop a screening program to test chemicals for their possible estrogenic and other endocrine effects. Shortly thereafter, the Chemical Guidelines Program of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development's (OECD) Environmental Directorate organized a Task Force on Endocrine Disruption Testing and Assessment to coordinate development of internationally harmonized screening and testing protocols. Most of the research devoted to this effort has focused on detecting impaired estrogenicity, androgenicity, and/or steroidogenesis, with little progress toward developing assays to detect chemicals that might interfere with thyroid function. Despite the fact that wildlife biologists have been reporting abnormal thyroid gland development and unusual thyroid hormone (TH) and retinoid ratios in fish and birds since the early 1960s, few studies have demonstrated an association between an environmental contaminant and a particular health end point other than reduced reproductive success at the population level. This article is a review of the literature that specifically examines THs and their role in normal behavior and development in wildlife. It presents several studies that associated changes in the thyroid gland, TH concentrations, and behavior with contaminant exposure. The goal of this article is to provide fodder for the creation of simple screens to detect possible thyroid system agonists and antagonists.

Title: Amphibian Metamorphosis Assay: Investigation of the potential effects of five chemicals on the hypothalamic-pituitary thyroid axis of Xenopus laevis
Snippet: Established in 1998, the purpose of the US Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program (EDSP) was to evaluate the potential for exposure to drinking water contaminants and pesticide chemicals to disrupt the endocrine systems of humans and/or wildlife. The EPA employs a tiered approach to screen chemicals for potential estrogenic, androgenic, and thyroid-related bioactivity (US EPA, 1998). Tier 1 comprises a battery of assays (five in vitro and six in vivo) which were developed for use as an integrated screening tool for potential endocrine bioactivity (US EPA, 2008a). Utilizing a weight-of-evidence (WoE) approach, chemicals that exhibit activity in screening assays are then considered for longer term in vivo Tier 2 tests which incorporate apical endpoints for identifying adverse effects, and to establish quantitative dose-response relationships needed for risk assessments (US EPA, 2021). 

The current EDSP Tier 1 battery includes three in vivo screening assays that feature thyroid-responsive endpoints: the rat male and female pubertal assays; and the Amphibian Metamorphosis Assay (AMA; US EPA, 2009). The AMA is a generalized vertebrate model that represents conserved structures and functions of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis. This assay is important because amphibian metamorphosis is a well-studied, thyroid-dependent process that responds to substances active within the HPT axis, and it is the only assay in the Tier 1 battery used to assess thyroid activity in animals during the process of morphological development (US EPA, 2009;OECD, 2009). Thyroid hormone (TH) is essential for the development and maintenance of normal vertebrate physiological functions, and delivery of TH to cells and tissues is highly regulated during early development and adult stages, which is governed by complex physiological processes that involve the HPT axis, extending to peripheral organs and tissues (Zoeller et al., 2007).

Title: Guidance for the identification of endocrine disruptors in the context of Regulations (EU) No 528/2012 and (EC) No 1107/2009
Snippet: Two standardised tests, the amphibian metamorphosis assay (AMA (OECD, 2009c)) and the larval growth and development assay (LAGDA (OECD, 2015d)) can be used to investigate potential endocrine adverse effects in amphibians. The AMA (OECD TG 231, level 3 of the OECD CF) is a validated amphibian mechanistic in vivo assay designed as a screening assay for potential thyroidal effects. The LAGDA (OECD TG 241, level 4 of the OECD CF) is more comprehensive, covering, in addition to thyroidal effects, other endocrine-disrupting effects on the development of the reproductive system, and allowing the evaluation of other types of developmental and reproductive toxicants. Test conditions and measured parameters are briefly described below and summarised in Table 16. Moreover, those tests also include the investigation of parameters that are not mechanistically specific for thyroid effects and might be sensitive to general toxicity. It has to be noted that water quality could impact the results, as common water pollutants like nitrates may also have thyroid effects in amphibians (Wang et al., 2015). Another level 3 test, the Xenopus embryonic thyroid signalling assay (XETA) is currently under validation for the detection of thyroid active substances.

Despite the fact that wildlife biologists have been reporting abnormal thyroid gland development and unusual thyroid hormone (TH) and retinoid ratios in fish and birds since the early 1960s, few studies have demonstrated an association between an environmental contaminant and a particular health end point other than reduced reproductive success at the population level. This article is a review of the literature that specifically examines THs and their role in normal behavior and development in wildlife. It presents several studies that associated changes in the thyroid gland, TH concentrations, and behavior with contaminant exposure. The goal of this article is to provide fodder for the creation of simple screens to detect possible thyroid system agonists and antagonists.

documents.title: Amphibian Metamorphosis Assay: Investigation of the potential effects of five chemicals on the hypothalamic-pituitary thyroid axis of Xenopus laevis
documents.snippet:
Established in 1998, the purpose of the US Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Endocrine Disruptor Screening Program (EDSP) was to evaluate the potential for exposure to drinking water contaminants and pesticide chemicals to disrupt the endocrine systems of humans and/or wildlife. The EPA employs a tiered approach to screen chemicals for potential estrogenic, androgenic, and thyroid-related bioactivity (US EPA, 1998). Tier 1 comprises a battery of assays (five in vitro and six in vivo) which were developed for use as an integrated screening tool for potential endocrine bioactivity (US EPA, 2008a). Utilizing a weight-of-evidence (WoE) approach, chemicals that exhibit activity in screening assays are then considered for longer term in vivo Tier 2 tests which incorporate apical endpoints for identifying adverse effects, and to establish quantitative dose-response relationships needed for risk assessments (US EPA, 2021). 

The current EDSP Tier 1 battery includes three in vivo screening assays that feature thyroid-responsive endpoints: the rat male and female pubertal assays; and the Amphibian Metamorphosis Assay (AMA; US EPA, 2009). The AMA is a generalized vertebrate model that represents conserved structures and functions of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid (HPT) axis. This assay is important because amphibian metamorphosis is a well-studied, thyroid-dependent process that responds to substances active within the HPT axis, and it is the only assay in the Tier 1 battery used to assess thyroid activity in animals during the process of morphological development (US EPA, 2009;OECD, 2009). Thyroid hormone (TH) is essential for the development and maintenance of normal vertebrate physiological functions, and delivery of TH to cells and tissues is highly regulated during early development and adult stages, which is governed by complex physiological processes that involve the HPT axis, extending to peripheral organs and tissues (Zoeller et al., 2007).

documents.title: Guidance for the identification of endocrine disruptors in the context of Regulations (EU) No 528/2012 and (EC) No 1107/2009
documents.snippet: Two standardised tests, the amphibian metamorphosis assay (AMA (OECD, 2009c)) and the larval growth and development assay (LAGDA (OECD, 2015d)) can be used to investigate potential endocrine adverse effects in amphibians. The AMA (OECD TG 231, level 3 of the OECD CF) is a validated amphibian mechanistic in vivo assay designed as a screening assay for potential thyroidal effects. The LAGDA (OECD TG 241, level 4 of the OECD CF) is more comprehensive, covering, in addition to thyroidal effects, other endocrine-disrupting effects on the development of the reproductive system, and allowing the evaluation of other types of developmental and reproductive toxicants. Test conditions and measured parameters are briefly described below and summarised in Table 16. Moreover, those tests also include the investigation of parameters that are not mechanistically specific for thyroid effects and might be sensitive to general toxicity. It has to be noted that water quality could impact the results, as common water pollutants like nitrates may also have thyroid effects in amphibians (Wang et al., 2015). Another level 3 test, the Xenopus embryonic thyroid signalling assay (XETA) is currently under validation for the detection of thyroid active substances.

attempts.answer:
# Overview

Regulatory assessment of endocrine disruption has evolved from broad in vivo screens to a harmonized, tiered system that integrates mechanistic in vitro assays, targeted in vivo screens for causal confirmation, and life-cycle/field-relevant tests, organized by endocrine pathways (estrogenic, androgenic, thyroid, steroidogenic) within the OECD Conceptual Framework and ECHA/EFSA guidance for endocrine-active substances (EATS) <cite id="141742aa-1">OECD and ECHA/EFSA frameworks standardize endocrine disruption testing across estrogenic, androgenic, thyroid, and steroidogenic modalities, using tiered strategies (REACH, EFSA) and weight-of-evidence approaches to minimize animal use while ensuring hazard identification</cite> <cite id="141742aa-2">ECHA/EFSA guidance structures evidence into levels (non-test information to mechanistic in vitro to in vivo adversity and back to refined in vitro adversity), and case workbooks show that fish (zebrafish/medaka) and amphibian in vivo studies can fulfill adversity and mechanistic endpoints for ED classification</cite> <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated methods cover EATS pathways; regulatory authorities require datasets that assess endocrine activity and adversity, with mechanistic in vitro and in vivo studies aligned to OECD Test Guideline 150 and ToxCast-type data</cite> <cite id="141742aa-4">Global programs (EDSP, EFSA for pesticides/biocides, Japan EXTEND2016) use tiered approaches from simple binding assays to multigenerational whole-animal tests; current tests span receptor assays to population-level life-cycle toxicity</cite>.

Below, we summarize historically used animal assays, which persist in current regulatory practice, and why some were retired while others endured.

# Historically used animal assays for endocrine disruption

Early programs relied on multi-endpoint rodent reproductive toxicology and species-specific screens, often preceded by short in vivo bioassays to flag activity before resource-intensive multigenerational studies <cite id="a8de5563-2">Historically, estrogenic activity was assessed via vaginal cornification, uterine water imbibition after a single dose, and uterine weight gain after repeated dosing; the latter (uterotrophic) was selected and validated by the OECD as the standardized estrogen screen</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-0">The OECD validation program formalized immature rat and adult ovariectomized rat uterotrophic assays using robust protocols transferable across labs, tested against potent ER agonists and antagonists, and demonstrated reproducibility for weak agonists</cite>. Amphibian assays targeting the HPT axis (e.g., Xenopus bladder/gonad histology and metamorphosis endpoints) provided thyroid-modality evidence and developmental adversity, while fish assays evaluated reproduction and sexual development across life stages <cite id="cb670e8b-2">Standardized amphibian thyroid assays include the amphibian metamorphosis assay (OECD TG 231) and larval amphibian growth and development assay (OECD TG 241), with XETA (OECD TG 248) detecting thyroid-active compounds via induction of fluorescence</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-4">OECD guidance expects non-mammalian vertebrates (teleosts and amphibians) to cover EATS; fish assays such as the short-term reproduction (TG 229), 21-day (TG 230), and sexual development (TG 234) tests, plus the amphibian metamorphosis assay (TG 231), are recommended modalities for estrogenic and thyroid effects</cite>.

In parallel, higher-tier chronic toxicity paradigms for amphibians and fish assessed full-life-cycle developmental and reproductive adversity under exposure conditions, typically triggered by positive lower-tier screens <cite id="cb670e8b-1">EDSTAC proposed an amphibian higher-tier chronic test if triggered by lower-tier screens and exposure characterization; a validated frog chronic test may be justified at Tier 3 if the substance is active in Tier 2 metamorphosis tests and the species/conditions are ecologically representative</cite>. For androgenic modalities, in vivo antiandrogen assays developed in rodents were used to detect AR antagonism and support hazard identification, later integrated into OECD guidance as mechanistic in vivo screens aligned with the uterotrophic paradigm <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated methods cover EATS modalities, including androgenic endpoints and assays; regulatory frameworks rely on mechanistic in vivo and in vitro data integrated via weight of evidence</cite>.

# Which assays persist in current regulatory use

- Estrogenic pathway (rodent uterotrophic screen):
  - The immature rat or adult/ovariectomized mouse/rat uterotrophic bioassay (OECD TG 440) remains a validated, internationally recognized short-term screen to identify ER agonists and prioritize compounds for further testing; it is explicitly recognized by OECD and U.S. EPA and is widely used to detect increases in uterine weight via ER-mediated water imbibition and proliferation <cite id="a8de5563-0">The OECD validation program established standardized protocols for immature rat and adult ovariectomized rat uterotrophic assays with robust reliability and interlaboratory transferability</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-1">OECD TG 440 was validated as a short-term in vivo estrogen screen; it is one of 11 Tier 1 assays in the EPA EDSP and considered the “gold standard” for ER agonists, measuring uterine weight increases in immature or ovariectomized rodents</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-2">The uterotrophic response (uterine weight gain after dosing) was selected among historical options (vaginal keratinization and single-dose water imbibition) as the standardized estrogen screen due to its robustness and transferability</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-4">Guidelines (OECD 2007; US EPA 2009a) describe conduct and performance specifications; the assay detects ER agonists by 3-day dosing in low-endocrine-background animals</cite>.

- Androgenic pathway (rodent Hershberger-type screen):
  - Rodent antiandrogen in vivo assays (Hershberger) persist as part of regulatory batteries to detect AR antagonism and support androgen-modality adversity decisions, integrated within OECD Test Guideline frameworks alongside estrogenic, thyroidal, and steroidogenic modalities <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated methods cover androgenic modalities within EATS; regulatory frameworks rely on standardized in vivo mechanistic assays and in vitro bioassays integrated by weight of evidence</cite> <cite id="141742aa-4">Tier 1 and Tier 2 EDSP tests include receptor binding assays and whole-animal adversity assays; the Hershberger-type paradigm supports androgenic adversity screening</cite>.

- Thyroidal pathway (amphibian and fish):
  - Amphibian thyroid assays are recognized to investigate T-modality adversity: OECD TG 231 (Amphibian Metamorphosis Assay) as a mechanistic in vivo screen and OECD TG 241 (Larval Amphibian Growth and Development Assay) for broader developmental adversity; OECD TG 248 (XETA) detects thyroid activity via fluorescent readouts and is under/accepted validation components <cite id="cb670e8b-2">ECHA/EFSA guidance recommends AMA (OECD TG 231) or, in specific circumstances, XETA (OECD TG 248); LAGDA (OECD TG 241) can fully investigate T-mediated adversity when appropriate</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-4">For non-mammalian vertebrates, OECD expects investigation of EATS using teleosts and amphibians; TG 229, 230, 234 for teleosts and TG 231 for amphibians are standard options</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-0">EFSA’s 2018 criteria and 2021 case-study framework accept AMA and XETA under defined conditions and evaluate extended protocols (EAMA) and new EPA LATT submissions within ongoing OECD validation</cite>.
  - Fish early-life reproductive toxicology assays (e.g., OECD TG 230, 234, 229) remain core to thyroid- and estrogenic-axis hazard identification for vertebrate wildlife, often replacing full-life-cycle tests when exposure is characterized and substances are active at lower tiers <cite id="141742aa-4">Current testing programs (EDSP, EFSA for pesticides/biocides) include tiered fish assays from short-term reproduction to multigenerational life cycle; early-life reproductive tests capture population-relevant endpoints efficiently</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-1">An amphibian higher-tier test may be triggered by lower-tier positives and exposure relevance; analogous fish chronic tests can be justified at Tier 3 when triggered and ecologically representative</cite>.

- Steroidogenic pathway (rodent and in vivo/ vitro integration):
  - The rat ovarian/uterine in vivo paradigm for steroidogenic disruption (e.g., ovary weight, folliculogenesis, cyclicity) persists for causal inference on ovulatory/ reproductive endpoints, complemented by in vitro steroidogenesis assays; together they map to EATS and adverse outcome pathways articulated in OECD guidance and EU regulations <cite id="141742aa-1">OECD test guidelines and EU REACH tiered strategies require standardized in vivo assays for reproductive endpoints across EATS; weight of evidence integrates multiple levels</cite> <cite id="141742aa-2">Case studies show integrated use of mammalian in vivo (rodent fish amphibian) and mechanistic in vitro (ToxCast) to assign MoA and adversity for EATS pathways</cite> <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated steroidogenic in vitro assays (e.g., OECD TG 456 and aromatase assays) complement in vivo adversity testing to reduce animals while maintaining mechanistic coverage</cite>.

- Cross-cutting in vivo life-cycle/field-relevant tests:
  - Multigenerational reproductive toxicity (rodent) and chronic in vivo tests in fish/amphibians continue as confirmatory adversity assays when mechanistic plausibility and exposure indicate potential population-level risk, particularly for pesticides and persistent chemicals <cite id="141742aa-4">EDSP’s Tier 2 uses whole-animal life cycle tests to assess potential adverse effects from endocrine MoAs; EU pesticide/biocide programs similarly require in vivo adversity under OECD frameworks</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-1">Higher-tier amphibian chronic tests are justified when lower-tier assays are positive and exposure is significant, with ecologically representative species and exposure characterization</cite>.

# Why some assays were retired or downgraded

- Mechanistic plausibility and specificity:
  - Bioassays lacking clear endocrine receptor linkage (e.g., vaginal cornification, generalized organ changes) were retired in favor of assays with defined receptor pathways and endpoint mapping to EATS, improving causal inference and assay portability across chemicals and species <cite id="a8de5563-2">The OECD EDTA selected the uterotrophic response over historical options like vaginal cornification due to mechanistic clarity (ER-mediated uterine water imbibition) and demonstrated transferability across species and labs</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-1">The uterotrophic assay became the gold standard ER agonist screen because its endpoint directly reflects ER-mediated proliferation and is robustly validated</cite>.
  - Amphibian thyroid assays were restructured from broad malformation screens to thyroid-specific, axis-mapped assays (AMA, XETA) to avoid confounding with general toxicity and to align with thyroid adversity decisions in ECHA/EFSA criteria <cite id="cb670e8b-2">ECHA/EFSA guidance recommends AMA for thyroid modality screening and LAGDA for broader developmental adversity, while XETA provides a mechanistic fluorescent readout of thyroid signaling</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-0">EFSA evaluated extended AMA protocols and EPA’s LATT submissions under the lens of thyroid adversity decision criteria, clarifying when new protocols can substitute or complement standard TGs</cite>.

- Harmonization, validation, and reproducibility:
  - Assays that failed interlaboratory validation or showed inconsistent sensitivity across species were retired or revalidated; the uterotrophic bioassay underwent extensive OECD-coordinated validation to ensure reliability and comparability across labs and routes of exposure, cementing its continued use <cite id="a8de5563-0">OECD validation for uterotrophic bioassay demonstrated robust transferability and reproducibility using reference ER agonists and antagonists, including for weak agonists across oral and subcutaneous routes</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-4">OECD and US EPA guidelines define assay conduct and performance specifications that standardize interpretation and ensure consistent detection of ER agonists</cite>.
  - Amphibian and fish higher-tier chronic tests were codified and tiered to improve relevance and efficiency; chronic amphibian tests are now deployed at Tier 3 only when lower-tier evidence and exposure relevance trigger their use, reducing unnecessary animal use while maintaining ecological protection <cite id="cb670e8b-1">Amphibian chronic tests are justified at Tier 3 when triggered by lower-tier screens and exposure data and use ecologically representative species to avoid redundancy with fish tests</cite>.

- Replacement by mechanistic in vitro assays and ToxCast:
  - Many historical in vivo screens were downgraded or retired as OECD/ECHA/US frameworks accepted validated in vitro assays for activity (e.g., yeast estrogen/androgen assays, luciferase-based reporter assays, and high-throughput ToxCast) that reduce animal use, provide MoA information, and integrate into AOP-based weight-of-evidence decisions; in vivo assays persist primarily to confirm adversity in intact organisms when required by regulatory tiers or when in vitro sufficiency criteria are unmet <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated EATS-specific in vitro assays (e.g., ToxCast and yeast bioassays) provide mechanistic data at level 2, reducing reliance on animal testing when sufficient to support adversity conclusions</cite> <cite id="141742aa-1">Regulatory frameworks emphasize integrating non-animal methods and in vitro data within tiered strategies to minimize animals while maintaining robust hazard identification across EATS pathways</cite> <cite id="141742aa-4">EDSP Tier 1 uses rapid receptor/alternative assays; Tier 2 escalates to whole-animal adversity only when endocrine activity is confirmed, aligning with animal reduction goals</cite>.
  - For thyroidal modalities, XETA and extended AMA protocols have been proposed and evaluated to replace labor-intensive histology with mechanistic fluorescent signaling readouts while preserving amphibian thyroid-axis relevance; agencies analyze power and interpretive criteria to ensure data sufficiency and consistency with adversity decisions <cite id="cb670e8b-2">XETA (OECD TG 248) detects thyroid-active compounds via induction of fluorescence compared to controls, offering a mechanistic assay alternative to histology for thyroid modality screening</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-0">EFSA compared extended AMA (EAMA) and EPA LATT protocols to standard AMA/LAGDA, evaluating statistical power and interpretive recommendations for thyroid histology changes under ECHA/EFSA criteria</cite>.

- Endpoint clarity and confounding:
  - Assays mixing multiple modes (e.g., broad developmental malformations in amphibians without thyroid-axis linkage) were retired or restricted to higher tiers to prevent confounding by general toxicity, contaminants, or water-quality factors; current TGs require thyroid-specific endpoints or explicit controls for non-specific effects and exposure conditions <cite id="cb670e8b-4">Amphibian assays (AMA, LAGDA) and fish assays (229/230/234) are aligned to specific EATS modalities to ensure endpoint specificity</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-2">ECHA/EFSA guidance emphasizes that XETA is targeted to detect thyroid-active compounds via specific fluorescence induction, avoiding non-specificity</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-4">Water quality can impact amphibian thyroid endpoints (e.g., nitrates), so test conditions and measured parameters include controls for non-mechanistic effects</cite>.

- Programmatic efficiency and regulatory alignment:
  - EDSP and EU programs formalized two-tier and tiered approaches that strategically escalate to in vivo adversity only when activity is established, reducing reliance on standalone chronic in vivo screens and enabling replacement of certain legacy assays with validated alternatives; agencies now favor multipurpose assays (e.g., ELSOT-style fish paradigms) that simultaneously probe multiple endocrine endpoints under ecologically realistic exposure <cite id="141742aa-4">Tier 1 uses rapid in vitro/binding assays and simple in vivo screens; Tier 2 then applies multigenerational or population-level tests only when endocrine activity is indicated, optimizing resource use</cite> <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD Test Guideline 150 and ECHA/EFSA guidance formalize integrated strategies where adversity is assessed using laboratory animals when necessary, but mechanistic in vitro data can substitute or reduce in vivo burden</cite>.
  - The absence of endocrine activity does not exempt from adversity assessment; when in vitro insufficiency persists, regulatory frameworks still require in vivo adversity testing for conclusive hazard identification, preserving the role of validated rodent and aquatic in vivo assays rather than wholesale elimination <cite id="141742aa-3">Authorities require datasets to permit conclusive assessment of endocrine disruptor status; if endocrine activity is absent or insufficient, adversity assessment in laboratory animals remains necessary per OECD guidance</cite>.

# Examples of retired or downgraded assays and their replacements

- Vaginal cornification/tear-drop/forelimb deformity paradigms (rodent/avian/amphibian): These historically served as estrogenic or developmental screens but lacked receptor specificity and suffered from species- and strain-specific confounders; they were retired in favor of uterotrophic ER-specific endpoints and standardized developmental toxicity paradigms, with amphibian thyroid assays replacing broad malformation screens for T-modality decisions <cite id="a8de5563-2">Historical estrogen screens (vaginal cornification, single-dose uterine water imbibition) were superseded by the uterotrophic assay selected by OECD for standardized ER activity detection due to robustness and transferability</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-2">Amphibian thyroid adversity is now investigated with standardized AMA (screen) and LAGDA (full adversity), with XETA replacing histology-based screens with a mechanistic fluorescent assay</cite>.

- Whole-animal chronic amphibian/fish assays as sole screens: These were downsized and tiered; chronic, full-life-cycle tests are reserved for Tier 3 when lower-tier screens and exposure data indicate risk, reducing redundant testing and improving ecological relevance; early-life fish assays (230/234) and amphibian LAGDA provide efficient adversity capture under controlled exposure <cite id="cb670e8b-1">Amphibian chronic tests are triggered by lower-tier positives and exposure characterization, with ecologically representative species to avoid redundancy with fish tests</cite> <cite id="141742aa-4">EDSP and EU programs deploy tiered fish assays and early-life reproductive tests to capture population-level adversity efficiently before full life-cycle studies</cite>.

- Non-mechanistic in vivo developmental malformations without endocrine linkage: These were deprecated in favor of thyroid-specific amphibian assays and fish HPT/HPG axis tests with mapped endpoints and exposure controls, as reflected in pesticide criteria and ECHA/EFSA guidance <cite id="cb670e8b-0">EFSA criteria accept AMA/XETA for thyroid adversity under defined conditions and evaluate extended protocols/LATT, clarifying when non-standard protocols can be used instead of traditional histology-based assays</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-4">OECD expects EATS coverage using teleosts and amphibians with specific TGs to determine endocrine activity and adversity, avoiding broad non-specific malformation endpoints</cite>.

# Why some assays survived (and how they are used today)

Surviving assays are those that (1) map directly to defined EATS modalities with mechanistic endpoints, (2) have demonstrated interlaboratory reliability and interpretive clarity, (3) provide decision-relevant adversity evidence efficiently within tiered frameworks, and (4) integrate with in vitro/NAMs in weight-of-evidence decisions. The uterotrophic estrogen screen and Hershberger antiandrogen paradigm remain because they provide rapid, species-relevant confirmation of ER/AR activity and adversity under controlled exposure, with harmonized OECD/EPA guidelines ensuring comparability and interpretability across jurisdictions <cite id="a8de5563-0">The OECD validation and interlaboratory reproducibility of uterotrophic protocols across routes and species underpin its regulatory acceptance</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-1">Its status as a validated OECD TG and EDSP Tier 1 “gold standard” reflects its mechanistic clarity and robust detection of ER agonists</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-4">Guidelines standardize design, dosing, and endpoint interpretation, enabling consistent performance specifications across labs</cite>. Amphibian and fish assays persisted and evolved to reflect ecological adversity pathways (metamorphosis, reproduction, sexual development) with thyroid-specific modalities and life-stage sensitivity, ensuring protection of wildlife endpoints while aligning with AOPs and exposure characterization <cite id="cb670e8b-2">Amphibian TGs (AMA for thyroid screening; LAGDA for broader adversity) and XETA mechanistic assay allow targeted thyroid adversity decisions</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-4">OECD expects teleost and amphibian assays to cover EATS with TGs such as 229/230/234 and 231 for reproductive and developmental toxicity under ecologically relevant exposure</cite>. Finally, rodent steroidogenic in vivo assays (ovarian/uterine) and in vitro steroidogenesis/androgen/estrogen assays coexist in a weight-of-evidence framework, with in vivo used to establish causal adversity and mechanistic sufficiency when required, and to calibrate AOP-based hazard identification <cite id="141742aa-1">OECD/ECHA tiered frameworks integrate mechanistic in vitro and in vivo adversity across EATS, using weight of evidence for hazard identification</cite> <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated steroidogenesis/aromatase assays complement in vivo adversity, reducing animals while maintaining mechanistic coverage</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Past animal tests spanned broad reproductive/developmental screens and species-specific bioassays; modern regulatory batteries retain mechanistic in vivo assays (uterotrophic estrogen, Hershberger antiandrogen, fish and amphibian reproductive/developmental toxicity) while retiring or tiering older, confounded screens and replacing them with validated in vitro assays and ToxCast/NAMs to reduce animals and improve mechanistic interpretability <cite id="a8de5563-2">Historical estrogen screens (vaginal cornification, uterine water imbibition) gave way to standardized uterotrophic ER assays due to mechanistic specificity and transferability</cite> <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD/ECHA frameworks now accept mechanistic in vitro assays (yeast/ToxCast) as Tier 1 evidence, escalating to in vivo adversity when necessary</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-2">Amphibian thyroid assays (AMA, LAGDA) and XETA have replaced broad histology-based screens with thyroid-specific endpoints and mechanistic readouts</cite>.
- Persistence hinges on mechanistic clarity, validation and reproducibility, alignment with EATS and AOPs, and efficiency within tiered regulatory strategies; retirement occurs when assays are confounded, non-reproducible across labs/species, or superseded by higher-specificity alternatives that still meet adversity relevance at lower tier levels <cite id="a8de5563-0">Interlaboratory validation and robust protocols have kept uterotrophic assays central</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-0">ECHA/EFSA criteria and OECD VMG evaluations drive replacement or acceptance of new amphibian/fish protocols based on power and interpretive clarity</cite> <cite id="141742aa-4">Tiered programs (EDSP, EU pesticides) escalate to whole-animal adversity only after positive lower-tier screens, preserving animal welfare while maintaining regulatory sufficiency</cite>.

Snippet: The widely accepted definition of an endocrine disruptor is "an exogenous substance or mixture that alters the function(s) of the endocrine system and consequently causes adverse health effects in an intact organism, or its progeny, or (sub)populations" (World Health Organisation/ International Programme on Chemical Safety [WHO/ IPCS], 2002). Title: The OECD program to validate the rat uterotrophic bioassay. Phase 2: dose-response studies.
Snippet: The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) initiated a highpriority activity in 1997 to revise existing guidelines and to develop new guidelines for the screening and testing of potential endocrine disrupters (OECD 1998a). One portion of the activity is to validate the rodent uterotrophic bioassay, an in vivo screen intended to identify compounds that are suspected agonists or antagonists of estrogen, and to assist the prioritization of positive compounds for further testing. In phase 1 of the validation program, standardized protocols were developed for two versions of the uterotrophic bioassay, the immature rat and the adult ovariectomized (OVX) rat. All protocols were robust, reproducible, and transferable across laboratories using these reference compounds (Kanno et al. 2001). Therefore, the VMG proceeded with the design and execution of phase 2 of the uterotrophic bioassay's validation program. 

A key objective of validation exercises is to demonstrate the reliability of the standardized protocols. Reliability includes a demonstration of the transferability of the protocols among laboratories and the reproducibility of the results from those protocols among laboratories. Such a demonstration is expected to employ test substances that represent the substances of likely concern in regulatory use, for example, in the case of the uterotrophic bioassay, weak estrogen-receptor agonists. This article compares the reproducibility of the dose responses of five weak estrogen agonists using four protocols that include both oral gavage and subcutaneous (sc) routes of administration.

Snippet: The activity is part of the OECD Test Guidelines Programme, so overall responsibility of the work lies with the Working Group of National Co-ordinators of the Test Guidelines Programme (WNT).

The assays include a) structural activity relationships and in vitro assays that would identify a chemical based on certain intrinsic characteristics (e.g., estrogen receptor binding affinity); b) short-term in vivo assays to demonstrate relevant activity in the intact animal (e.g., the uterotrophic assay); and c) long-term assays involving exposure to the test substance at different stages of the development of the animal (e.g., the two-generation reproductive assay). The OECD strategy aims to develop these assays as multipurpose tools rather than as a rigid scheme. The purpose and use of a bioassay could vary depending on the chemical substance and the available toxicological data on that chemical. An early screen in one case could become a means to determine a chemical's mode of action in another (5). 

In this article we focus on the OECD validation program for an in vivo screen for estrogenic activity. Historically, several candidate systems are available: a vaginal cornification and keratinization response (6), a water imbibition response of the uterus after a single dose of the test compound (7), and a uterine tissue weight increase after several doses of the test compound (8)(9)(10). The EDTA reached consensus to select the latter assay, called the uterotrophic assay, for further development and validation. The uterotrophic response has been employed to evaluate estrogenic activity using a number of mammalian and avian species, although primarily laboratory rodents. Because the rat has become the preferred species for reproductive and developmental toxicity testing, we chose it as the test species for further standardization and development of the uterotrophic assay.

Snippet: The rodent uterotrophic assay is a short-term, in vivo screening assay designed to detect compounds with potential estrogenic activity (i.e., ER agonists) by measuring a compound's ability to produce an increase in uterine weight. Test guidelines (OECD, 2007;US EPA, 2009a) are available that describe the conduct, interpretation, and performance specifications for the uterotrophic assay. The guideline assay uses immature female rats or ovariectomized adult rats (or mice), which have low levels of endogenous estrogens (Reel et al., 1996) and therefore, low baseline uterine weights. If using ovariectomized females, complete ovariectomy must be confirmed before initiation of dosing by evaluating vaginal cytology for 5 days to confirm the absence of cycling. Rats should show cytologic evidence of diestrus during this time, indicating successful ovariectomy, and subsequently indicating basal levels of endogenous estrogens are too low to induce cycling. Title: The assessment for potential thyroid‐mediated endocrine disruption in amphibians: Clarification on the use of new methods and on the interpretation of changes in thyroid histology
Snippet: According to Commission Regulation (EU) 2018/605 laying down the scientific criteria for the hazard identification of pesticides having endocrine-disrupting properties, scientific data generated in accordance with internationally agreed study protocols should be considered. 

The ECHA/EFSA guidance on hazard identification of endocrine disruptors (ED) recommends a test according to OECD 231 (amphibian metamorphosis assay (AMA)) or, in specific circumstances, a test according to OECD test guideline (TG) 248 (Xenopus Eleutheroembryonic Thyroid Assay (XETA)) for the full investigation of endocrine activity through thyroid (T) modality in non-mammalian species. T-mediated endocrine adversity is fully investigated when a test according to OECD TG 241 (larval amphibian growth and development assay (LAGDA)) is available. In 2021, Ortego et al. (2021) published a protocol in which the standard AMA (TG 231) was proposed to be extended until animals reached stage Nieuwkoop and Faber (NF) 62, calling it the extended amphibian metamorphosis assay (EAMA). Several studies using this protocol have already been submitted in dossiers for the approval of pesticide active substances. 

In addition, in 2024, the US EPA presented another amphibian protocol, the larval amphibian toxicity test (LATT), to the OECD Validation Management Group for ecotoxicity testing (OECD VMGeco). 

Following the publication by Ortego et al. (2021) and the submission of studies in line with its protocol in pesticide dossiers, along with the ongoing work at OECD, EFSA compared the new proposed methods to the available standard protocols, i.e. AMA and LAGDA. This comparison should include a power analysis of the main diagnostic parameter(s) and growth parameters and consider the advantages and disadvantages of available standard and non-standard protocols. Moreover, EFSA provided interpretative recommendations related to changes in the thyroid histology of amphibians.

Title: Guidance for the identification of endocrine disruptors in the context of Regulations (EU) No 528/2012 and (EC) No 1107/2009
Snippet: Two standardised tests, the amphibian metamorphosis assay (AMA (OECD, 2009c)) and the larval growth and development assay (LAGDA (OECD, 2015d)) can be used to investigate potential endocrine adverse effects in amphibians. The AMA (OECD TG 231, level 3 of the OECD CF) is a validated amphibian mechanistic in vivo assay designed as a screening assay for potential thyroidal effects. The LAGDA (OECD TG 241, level 4 of the OECD CF) is more comprehensive, covering, in addition to thyroidal effects, other endocrine-disrupting effects on the development of the reproductive system, and allowing the evaluation of other types of developmental and reproductive toxicants. Moreover, those tests also include the investigation of parameters that are not mechanistically specific for thyroid effects and might be sensitive to general toxicity. It has to be noted that water quality could impact the results, as common water pollutants like nitrates may also have thyroid effects in amphibians (Wang et al., 2015). Another level 3 test, the Xenopus embryonic thyroid signalling assay (XETA) is currently under validation for the detection of thyroid active substances.

# Overview

Regulatory assessment of endocrine disruption has evolved from broad in vivo screens to a harmonized, tiered system that integrates mechanistic in vitro assays, targeted in vivo screens for causal confirmation, and life-cycle/field-relevant tests, organized by endocrine pathways (estrogenic, androgenic, thyroid, steroidogenic) within the OECD Conceptual Framework and ECHA/EFSA guidance for endocrine-active substances (EATS) <cite id="141742aa-1">OECD and ECHA/EFSA frameworks standardize endocrine disruption testing across estrogenic, androgenic, thyroid, and steroidogenic modalities, using tiered strategies (REACH, EFSA) and weight-of-evidence approaches to minimize animal use while ensuring hazard identification</cite> <cite id="141742aa-2">ECHA/EFSA guidance structures evidence into levels (non-test information to mechanistic in vitro to in vivo adversity and back to refined in vitro adversity), and case workbooks show that fish (zebrafish/medaka) and amphibian in vivo studies can fulfill adversity and mechanistic endpoints for ED classification</cite> <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated methods cover EATS pathways; regulatory authorities require datasets that assess endocrine activity and adversity, with mechanistic in vitro and in vivo studies aligned to OECD Test Guideline 150 and ToxCast-type data</cite> <cite id="141742aa-4">Global programs (EDSP, EFSA for pesticides/biocides, Japan EXTEND2016) use tiered approaches from simple binding assays to multigenerational whole-animal tests; current tests span receptor assays to population-level life-cycle toxicity</cite>.

Below, we summarize historically used animal assays, which persist in current regulatory practice, and why some were retired while others endured.

# Historically used animal assays for endocrine disruption

Early programs relied on multi-endpoint rodent reproductive toxicology and species-specific screens, often preceded by short in vivo bioassays to flag activity before resource-intensive multigenerational studies <cite id="a8de5563-2">Historically, estrogenic activity was assessed via vaginal cornification, uterine water imbibition after a single dose, and uterine weight gain after repeated dosing; the latter (uterotrophic) was selected and validated by the OECD as the standardized estrogen screen</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-0">The OECD validation program formalized immature rat and adult ovariectomized rat uterotrophic assays using robust protocols transferable across labs, tested against potent ER agonists and antagonists, and demonstrated reproducibility for weak agonists</cite>. Amphibian assays targeting the HPT axis (e.g., Xenopus bladder/gonad histology and metamorphosis endpoints) provided thyroid-modality evidence and developmental adversity, while fish assays evaluated reproduction and sexual development across life stages <cite id="cb670e8b-2">Standardized amphibian thyroid assays include the amphibian metamorphosis assay (OECD TG 231) and larval amphibian growth and development assay (OECD TG 241), with XETA (OECD TG 248) detecting thyroid-active compounds via induction of fluorescence</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-4">OECD guidance expects non-mammalian vertebrates (teleosts and amphibians) to cover EATS; fish assays such as the short-term reproduction (TG 229), 21-day (TG 230), and sexual development (TG 234) tests, plus the amphibian metamorphosis assay (TG 231), are recommended modalities for estrogenic and thyroid effects</cite>.

In parallel, higher-tier chronic toxicity paradigms for amphibians and fish assessed full-life-cycle developmental and reproductive adversity under exposure conditions, typically triggered by positive lower-tier screens <cite id="cb670e8b-1">EDSTAC proposed an amphibian higher-tier chronic test if triggered by lower-tier screens and exposure characterization; a validated frog chronic test may be justified at Tier 3 if the substance is active in Tier 2 metamorphosis tests and the species/conditions are ecologically representative</cite>. For androgenic modalities, in vivo antiandrogen assays developed in rodents were used to detect AR antagonism and support hazard identification, later integrated into OECD guidance as mechanistic in vivo screens aligned with the uterotrophic paradigm <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated methods cover EATS modalities, including androgenic endpoints and assays; regulatory frameworks rely on mechanistic in vivo and in vitro data integrated via weight of evidence</cite>.

# Which assays persist in current regulatory use

- Estrogenic pathway (rodent uterotrophic screen):
  - The immature rat or adult/ovariectomized mouse/rat uterotrophic bioassay (OECD TG 440) remains a validated, internationally recognized short-term screen to identify ER agonists and prioritize compounds for further testing; it is explicitly recognized by OECD and U.S. EPA and is widely used to detect increases in uterine weight via ER-mediated water imbibition and proliferation <cite id="a8de5563-0">The OECD validation program established standardized protocols for immature rat and adult ovariectomized rat uterotrophic assays with robust reliability and interlaboratory transferability</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-1">OECD TG 440 was validated as a short-term in vivo estrogen screen; it is one of 11 Tier 1 assays in the EPA EDSP and considered the “gold standard” for ER agonists, measuring uterine weight increases in immature or ovariectomized rodents</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-2">The uterotrophic response (uterine weight gain after dosing) was selected among historical options (vaginal keratinization and single-dose water imbibition) as the standardized estrogen screen due to its robustness and transferability</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-4">Guidelines (OECD 2007; US EPA 2009a) describe conduct and performance specifications; the assay detects ER agonists by 3-day dosing in low-endocrine-background animals</cite>.

- Androgenic pathway (rodent Hershberger-type screen):
  - Rodent antiandrogen in vivo assays (Hershberger) persist as part of regulatory batteries to detect AR antagonism and support androgen-modality adversity decisions, integrated within OECD Test Guideline frameworks alongside estrogenic, thyroidal, and steroidogenic modalities <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated methods cover androgenic modalities within EATS; regulatory frameworks rely on standardized in vivo mechanistic assays and in vitro bioassays integrated by weight of evidence</cite> <cite id="141742aa-4">Tier 1 and Tier 2 EDSP tests include receptor binding assays and whole-animal adversity assays; the Hershberger-type paradigm supports androgenic adversity screening</cite>.

- Thyroidal pathway (amphibian and fish):
  - Amphibian thyroid assays are recognized to investigate T-modality adversity: OECD TG 231 (Amphibian Metamorphosis Assay) as a mechanistic in vivo screen and OECD TG 241 (Larval Amphibian Growth and Development Assay) for broader developmental adversity; OECD TG 248 (XETA) detects thyroid activity via fluorescent readouts and is under/accepted validation components <cite id="cb670e8b-2">ECHA/EFSA guidance recommends AMA (OECD TG 231) or, in specific circumstances, XETA (OECD TG 248); LAGDA (OECD TG 241) can fully investigate T-mediated adversity when appropriate</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-4">For non-mammalian vertebrates, OECD expects investigation of EATS using teleosts and amphibians; TG 229, 230, 234 for teleosts and TG 231 for amphibians are standard options</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-0">EFSA’s 2018 criteria and 2021 case-study framework accept AMA and XETA under defined conditions and evaluate extended protocols (EAMA) and new EPA LATT submissions within ongoing OECD validation</cite>.
  - Fish early-life reproductive toxicology assays (e.g., OECD TG 230, 234, 229) remain core to thyroid- and estrogenic-axis hazard identification for vertebrate wildlife, often replacing full-life-cycle tests when exposure is characterized and substances are active at lower tiers <cite id="141742aa-4">Current testing programs (EDSP, EFSA for pesticides/biocides) include tiered fish assays from short-term reproduction to multigenerational life cycle; early-life reproductive tests capture population-relevant endpoints efficiently</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-1">An amphibian higher-tier test may be triggered by lower-tier positives and exposure relevance; analogous fish chronic tests can be justified at Tier 3 when triggered and ecologically representative</cite>.

- Steroidogenic pathway (rodent and in vivo/ vitro integration):
  - The rat ovarian/uterine in vivo paradigm for steroidogenic disruption (e.g., ovary weight, folliculogenesis, cyclicity) persists for causal inference on ovulatory/ reproductive endpoints, complemented by in vitro steroidogenesis assays; together they map to EATS and adverse outcome pathways articulated in OECD guidance and EU regulations <cite id="141742aa-1">OECD test guidelines and EU REACH tiered strategies require standardized in vivo assays for reproductive endpoints across EATS; weight of evidence integrates multiple levels</cite> <cite id="141742aa-2">Case studies show integrated use of mammalian in vivo (rodent fish amphibian) and mechanistic in vitro (ToxCast) to assign MoA and adversity for EATS pathways</cite> <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated steroidogenic in vitro assays (e.g., OECD TG 456 and aromatase assays) complement in vivo adversity testing to reduce animals while maintaining mechanistic coverage</cite>.

- Cross-cutting in vivo life-cycle/field-relevant tests:
  - Multigenerational reproductive toxicity (rodent) and chronic in vivo tests in fish/amphibians continue as confirmatory adversity assays when mechanistic plausibility and exposure indicate potential population-level risk, particularly for pesticides and persistent chemicals <cite id="141742aa-4">EDSP’s Tier 2 uses whole-animal life cycle tests to assess potential adverse effects from endocrine MoAs; EU pesticide/biocide programs similarly require in vivo adversity under OECD frameworks</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-1">Higher-tier amphibian chronic tests are justified when lower-tier assays are positive and exposure is significant, with ecologically representative species and exposure characterization</cite>.

# Why some assays were retired or downgraded

- Mechanistic plausibility and specificity:
  - Bioassays lacking clear endocrine receptor linkage (e.g., vaginal cornification, generalized organ changes) were retired in favor of assays with defined receptor pathways and endpoint mapping to EATS, improving causal inference and assay portability across chemicals and species <cite id="a8de5563-2">The OECD EDTA selected the uterotrophic response over historical options like vaginal cornification due to mechanistic clarity (ER-mediated uterine water imbibition) and demonstrated transferability across species and labs</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-1">The uterotrophic assay became the gold standard ER agonist screen because its endpoint directly reflects ER-mediated proliferation and is robustly validated</cite>.
  - Amphibian thyroid assays were restructured from broad malformation screens to thyroid-specific, axis-mapped assays (AMA, XETA) to avoid confounding with general toxicity and to align with thyroid adversity decisions in ECHA/EFSA criteria <cite id="cb670e8b-2">ECHA/EFSA guidance recommends AMA for thyroid modality screening and LAGDA for broader developmental adversity, while XETA provides a mechanistic fluorescent readout of thyroid signaling</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-0">EFSA evaluated extended AMA protocols and EPA’s LATT submissions under the lens of thyroid adversity decision criteria, clarifying when new protocols can substitute or complement standard TGs</cite>.

- Harmonization, validation, and reproducibility:
  - Assays that failed interlaboratory validation or showed inconsistent sensitivity across species were retired or revalidated; the uterotrophic bioassay underwent extensive OECD-coordinated validation to ensure reliability and comparability across labs and routes of exposure, cementing its continued use <cite id="a8de5563-0">OECD validation for uterotrophic bioassay demonstrated robust transferability and reproducibility using reference ER agonists and antagonists, including for weak agonists across oral and subcutaneous routes</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-4">OECD and US EPA guidelines define assay conduct and performance specifications that standardize interpretation and ensure consistent detection of ER agonists</cite>.
  - Amphibian and fish higher-tier chronic tests were codified and tiered to improve relevance and efficiency; chronic amphibian tests are now deployed at Tier 3 only when lower-tier evidence and exposure relevance trigger their use, reducing unnecessary animal use while maintaining ecological protection <cite id="cb670e8b-1">Amphibian chronic tests are justified at Tier 3 when triggered by lower-tier screens and exposure data and use ecologically representative species to avoid redundancy with fish tests</cite>.

- Replacement by mechanistic in vitro assays and ToxCast:
  - Many historical in vivo screens were downgraded or retired as OECD/ECHA/US frameworks accepted validated in vitro assays for activity (e.g., yeast estrogen/androgen assays, luciferase-based reporter assays, and high-throughput ToxCast) that reduce animal use, provide MoA information, and integrate into AOP-based weight-of-evidence decisions; in vivo assays persist primarily to confirm adversity in intact organisms when required by regulatory tiers or when in vitro sufficiency criteria are unmet <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated EATS-specific in vitro assays (e.g., ToxCast and yeast bioassays) provide mechanistic data at level 2, reducing reliance on animal testing when sufficient to support adversity conclusions</cite> <cite id="141742aa-1">Regulatory frameworks emphasize integrating non-animal methods and in vitro data within tiered strategies to minimize animals while maintaining robust hazard identification across EATS pathways</cite> <cite id="141742aa-4">EDSP Tier 1 uses rapid receptor/alternative assays; Tier 2 escalates to whole-animal adversity only when endocrine activity is confirmed, aligning with animal reduction goals</cite>.
  - For thyroidal modalities, XETA and extended AMA protocols have been proposed and evaluated to replace labor-intensive histology with mechanistic fluorescent signaling readouts while preserving amphibian thyroid-axis relevance; agencies analyze power and interpretive criteria to ensure data sufficiency and consistency with adversity decisions <cite id="cb670e8b-2">XETA (OECD TG 248) detects thyroid-active compounds via induction of fluorescence compared to controls, offering a mechanistic assay alternative to histology for thyroid modality screening</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-0">EFSA compared extended AMA (EAMA) and EPA LATT protocols to standard AMA/LAGDA, evaluating statistical power and interpretive recommendations for thyroid histology changes under ECHA/EFSA criteria</cite>.

- Endpoint clarity and confounding:
  - Assays mixing multiple modes (e.g., broad developmental malformations in amphibians without thyroid-axis linkage) were retired or restricted to higher tiers to prevent confounding by general toxicity, contaminants, or water-quality factors; current TGs require thyroid-specific endpoints or explicit controls for non-specific effects and exposure conditions <cite id="cb670e8b-4">Amphibian assays (AMA, LAGDA) and fish assays (229/230/234) are aligned to specific EATS modalities to ensure endpoint specificity</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-2">ECHA/EFSA guidance emphasizes that XETA is targeted to detect thyroid-active compounds via specific fluorescence induction, avoiding non-specificity</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-4">Water quality can impact amphibian thyroid endpoints (e.g., nitrates), so test conditions and measured parameters include controls for non-mechanistic effects</cite>.

- Programmatic efficiency and regulatory alignment:
  - EDSP and EU programs formalized two-tier and tiered approaches that strategically escalate to in vivo adversity only when activity is established, reducing reliance on standalone chronic in vivo screens and enabling replacement of certain legacy assays with validated alternatives; agencies now favor multipurpose assays (e.g., ELSOT-style fish paradigms) that simultaneously probe multiple endocrine endpoints under ecologically realistic exposure <cite id="141742aa-4">Tier 1 uses rapid in vitro/binding assays and simple in vivo screens; Tier 2 then applies multigenerational or population-level tests only when endocrine activity is indicated, optimizing resource use</cite> <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD Test Guideline 150 and ECHA/EFSA guidance formalize integrated strategies where adversity is assessed using laboratory animals when necessary, but mechanistic in vitro data can substitute or reduce in vivo burden</cite>.
  - The absence of endocrine activity does not exempt from adversity assessment; when in vitro insufficiency persists, regulatory frameworks still require in vivo adversity testing for conclusive hazard identification, preserving the role of validated rodent and aquatic in vivo assays rather than wholesale elimination <cite id="141742aa-3">Authorities require datasets to permit conclusive assessment of endocrine disruptor status; if endocrine activity is absent or insufficient, adversity assessment in laboratory animals remains necessary per OECD guidance</cite>.

# Examples of retired or downgraded assays and their replacements

- Vaginal cornification/tear-drop/forelimb deformity paradigms (rodent/avian/amphibian): These historically served as estrogenic or developmental screens but lacked receptor specificity and suffered from species- and strain-specific confounders; they were retired in favor of uterotrophic ER-specific endpoints and standardized developmental toxicity paradigms, with amphibian thyroid assays replacing broad malformation screens for T-modality decisions <cite id="a8de5563-2">Historical estrogen screens (vaginal cornification, single-dose uterine water imbibition) were superseded by the uterotrophic assay selected by OECD for standardized ER activity detection due to robustness and transferability</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-2">Amphibian thyroid adversity is now investigated with standardized AMA (screen) and LAGDA (full adversity), with XETA replacing histology-based screens with a mechanistic fluorescent assay</cite>.

- Whole-animal chronic amphibian/fish assays as sole screens: These were downsized and tiered; chronic, full-life-cycle tests are reserved for Tier 3 when lower-tier screens and exposure data indicate risk, reducing redundant testing and improving ecological relevance; early-life fish assays (230/234) and amphibian LAGDA provide efficient adversity capture under controlled exposure <cite id="cb670e8b-1">Amphibian chronic tests are triggered by lower-tier positives and exposure characterization, with ecologically representative species to avoid redundancy with fish tests</cite> <cite id="141742aa-4">EDSP and EU programs deploy tiered fish assays and early-life reproductive tests to capture population-level adversity efficiently before full life-cycle studies</cite>.

- Non-mechanistic in vivo developmental malformations without endocrine linkage: These were deprecated in favor of thyroid-specific amphibian assays and fish HPT/HPG axis tests with mapped endpoints and exposure controls, as reflected in pesticide criteria and ECHA/EFSA guidance <cite id="cb670e8b-0">EFSA criteria accept AMA/XETA for thyroid adversity under defined conditions and evaluate extended protocols/LATT, clarifying when non-standard protocols can be used instead of traditional histology-based assays</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-4">OECD expects EATS coverage using teleosts and amphibians with specific TGs to determine endocrine activity and adversity, avoiding broad non-specific malformation endpoints</cite>.

# Why some assays survived (and how they are used today)

Surviving assays are those that (1) map directly to defined EATS modalities with mechanistic endpoints, (2) have demonstrated interlaboratory reliability and interpretive clarity, (3) provide decision-relevant adversity evidence efficiently within tiered frameworks, and (4) integrate with in vitro/NAMs in weight-of-evidence decisions. The uterotrophic estrogen screen and Hershberger antiandrogen paradigm remain because they provide rapid, species-relevant confirmation of ER/AR activity and adversity under controlled exposure, with harmonized OECD/EPA guidelines ensuring comparability and interpretability across jurisdictions <cite id="a8de5563-0">The OECD validation and interlaboratory reproducibility of uterotrophic protocols across routes and species underpin its regulatory acceptance</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-1">Its status as a validated OECD TG and EDSP Tier 1 “gold standard” reflects its mechanistic clarity and robust detection of ER agonists</cite> <cite id="a8de5563-4">Guidelines standardize design, dosing, and endpoint interpretation, enabling consistent performance specifications across labs</cite>. Amphibian and fish assays persisted and evolved to reflect ecological adversity pathways (metamorphosis, reproduction, sexual development) with thyroid-specific modalities and life-stage sensitivity, ensuring protection of wildlife endpoints while aligning with AOPs and exposure characterization <cite id="cb670e8b-2">Amphibian TGs (AMA for thyroid screening; LAGDA for broader adversity) and XETA mechanistic assay allow targeted thyroid adversity decisions</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-4">OECD expects teleost and amphibian assays to cover EATS with TGs such as 229/230/234 and 231 for reproductive and developmental toxicity under ecologically relevant exposure</cite>. Finally, rodent steroidogenic in vivo assays (ovarian/uterine) and in vitro steroidogenesis/androgen/estrogen assays coexist in a weight-of-evidence framework, with in vivo used to establish causal adversity and mechanistic sufficiency when required, and to calibrate AOP-based hazard identification <cite id="141742aa-1">OECD/ECHA tiered frameworks integrate mechanistic in vitro and in vivo adversity across EATS, using weight of evidence for hazard identification</cite> <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD validated steroidogenesis/aromatase assays complement in vivo adversity, reducing animals while maintaining mechanistic coverage</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Past animal tests spanned broad reproductive/developmental screens and species-specific bioassays; modern regulatory batteries retain mechanistic in vivo assays (uterotrophic estrogen, Hershberger antiandrogen, fish and amphibian reproductive/developmental toxicity) while retiring or tiering older, confounded screens and replacing them with validated in vitro assays and ToxCast/NAMs to reduce animals and improve mechanistic interpretability <cite id="a8de5563-2">Historical estrogen screens (vaginal cornification, uterine water imbibition) gave way to standardized uterotrophic ER assays due to mechanistic specificity and transferability</cite> <cite id="141742aa-3">OECD/ECHA frameworks now accept mechanistic in vitro assays (yeast/ToxCast) as Tier 1 evidence, escalating to in vivo adversity when necessary</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-2">Amphibian thyroid assays (AMA, LAGDA) and XETA have replaced broad histology-based screens with thyroid-specific endpoints and mechanistic readouts</cite>.
- Persistence hinges on mechanistic clarity, validation and reproducibility, alignment with EATS and AOPs, and efficiency within tiered regulatory strategies; retirement occurs when assays are confounded, non-reproducible across labs/species, or superseded by higher-specificity alternatives that still meet adversity relevance at lower tier levels <cite id="a8de5563-0">Interlaboratory validation and robust protocols have kept uterotrophic assays central</cite> <cite id="cb670e8b-0">ECHA/EFSA criteria and OECD VMG evaluations drive replacement or acceptance of new amphibian/fish protocols based on power and interpretive clarity</cite> <cite id="141742aa-4">Tiered programs (EDSP, EU pesticides) escalate to whole-animal adversity only after positive lower-tier screens, preserving animal welfare while maintaining regulatory sufficiency</cite>. </answer>
